memory_lessons.applicability: This T1 workload and measurement setup; results may not generalize to other targets or runs.
memory_lessons.claim: The correct 4096-cap candidate measured 0.000289782 s, while the 8192- and 16384-partial candidates measured 0.000459449 s and 0.000473368 s respectively. The observed results do not support assuming that increasing partial count improves full-call time.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the proposed 2048-cap candidate with full-call timing and the required correctness checks.

proposal.hypothesis: The fastest observed correct T1 candidate used at most 4096 partials (0.000289782 s), while the 8192- and 16384-partial candidates were slower. This candidate targets one partial per 8192 inputs and caps the count at 2048, halving the maximum finalizer fan-in and partial writes versus the 4096-cap candidate, while doubling the largest per-CTA chunk. It tests whether that lower overhead still provides enough large-input parallelism; no speedup is assumed.

retained: Fuse fabsf(input[i]) into a first-stage contiguous scalar-load sum, using 256-thread CUB BlockReduce per CTA.
Choose partial_count = ceil(n/8192), capped at 2048; proportionally partition all input elements into contiguous CTA chunks.
Use one final 256-thread CTA to reduce every current-call partial and overwrite the output; explicitly overwrite output with zero when n is non-positive.
